Seminar 3 · Conditional probability and Bayes

## Sample Spaces and Events {.stage-slide #space-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
Roll two dice and every possible result is on the board. The sample space $\Omega$ is that whole board, and an **event** is any part of it you can point at.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="space-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="space-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="space-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="space-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
When every outcome is equally likely, a probability is a count. $P(\color{#93C54B}{A})$ is the cells in $\color{#93C54B}{A}$ over the cells in $\Omega$. Two fair dice earn that assumption, and most real problems do not.
:::

## Unions, Intersections and Complements {.stage-slide #setops-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
Two events on the same board. $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}$ is "either", $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}$ is "both", and $\color{#93C54B}{A}^{c}$ is everything left over.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="setops-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="setops-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="setops-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="setops-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
Add 6 and 18 and you get 24, which is three too many. The cells that belong to both events were counted twice, so they have to come back off.
:::

## The Same Picture, Drawn as Circles {.stage-slide #venn-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
A **Venn diagram** is the board with the grid rubbed out. The four counts are the ones you just read off it, and they still add to 36.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="venn-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="venn-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="venn-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="venn-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
These circles are drawn to scale, so $\color{#325D88}{B}$ really does cover three times the area of $\color{#93C54B}{A}$. Most are not, which is why the counts written on them matter more than the picture.
:::

## Set Notation for Probability {.formula-slide #set-formal}

::: {.lede-min}
Counting gives $P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = |\color{#93C54B}{A}|/|\Omega|$ and $P(\color{#93C54B}{A}^{c}) = 1 - P(\color{#93C54B}{A})$. Two rules do the rest.
:::

:::: {.fragment}
::: {.rule-label .rule-or}
[Either]{.rw} · $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}$
:::

$$\begin{array}{@{}l@{\;\;}c@{\;\;}l@{}}
P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}) & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) + P(\color{#325D88}{B}) - P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})\\[4pt]
\phantom{P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})} & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) + P(\color{#325D88}{B}) \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{if mutually exclusive}}
\end{array}$$
::::

:::: {.fragment}
::: {.rule-label .rule-and}
[Both]{.rw} · $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}$
:::

$$\begin{array}{@{}l@{\;\;}c@{\;\;}l@{}}
P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}) & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) \times P(\color{#325D88}{B} \mid \color{#93C54B}{A})\\[4pt]
\phantom{P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})} & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) \times P(\color{#325D88}{B}) \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{if independent}}
\end{array}$$
::::

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
Mutually exclusive means $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B} = \varnothing$, so there is nothing to subtract. Independent means learning $\color{#93C54B}{A}$ tells you nothing about $\color{#325D88}{B}$, which the next slide makes precise.
:::

## Conditioning Narrows the Sample Space {.stage-slide #cond-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
Eight in ten office managers would buy the software ($\color{#93C54B}{A}$), and four in ten of those would also upgrade ($\color{#325D88}{B}$). Of the rest, one in ten would. Given $\color{#325D88}{B}$, how likely is $\color{#93C54B}{A}$?
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="cond-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cond-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cond-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cond-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
Learning $\color{#325D88}{B}$ throws the other 66% away, so $P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \mid \color{#325D88}{B}) = P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})/P(\color{#325D88}{B})$.
:::

## Librarian or Farmer? {.stage-slide #bayes-hook}

::: {.lede-min}
Steve is very shy and withdrawn, invariably helpful but with very little interest in people or in the world of reality. A meek and tidy soul, he has a need for order and structure, and a passion for detail.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-prior}
<div id="prior-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="prior-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="prior-frag-2"}

::: {.slide-footer}
The description never changes; the answer does — because of a number that is not in it. That number is the base rate, and the next slide goes and counts it.
:::

## Twenty Farmers for Every Librarian {.stage-slide #bayes-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-bayes}
<div id="bayes-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-3"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-4"}

::: {.slide-footer}
The base rate is how common each job is, before you read a word about Steve. His description fits librarians four times better. But there are twenty times more farmers, so he is still five times more likely to be one.
:::

## Move the Prior, Watch the Answer Move {.sim-slide #bayes-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 3 · the base rate does the work
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
prior <- 1 / 21 # <-- P(librarian)
n <- 300000

lib  <- runif(n) < prior

# fits 40% of librarians, 10% of farmers
fits <- runif(n) < ifelse(lib, 0.40, 0.10)

c("P(H)" = prior, "P(H|E)" = mean(lib[fits]))
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
The evidence is identical every time — only the prior changes. `1/21` is the real ratio, one librarian for every twenty farmers; at `0.50` you get 0.80. **The description never had an opinion about how common librarians are, so the base rate has to supply it.**
:::

## Monty Hall Problem {.stage-slide #monty}

::: {.lede-min}
A car sits behind one of three doors and a goat behind each of the others. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door 3 on a goat and offers you the swap. Do you take it?
:::
